**The LFS target population** is all persons aged 15 and older whose usual place of residence is in Canada. That includes non-permanent residents, permanent residents and the Canadian-born.

**Excluded from the target population:**
- People living on reserves
- Full-time members of the regular Armed Forces
- People living in institutions, such as inmates of penal institutions and patients in hospitals and nursing homes

- **Labour Force Survey (LFS): mandatory.** Participation is mandatory for adults under the authority of the Statistics Act.
- **Canadian Income Survey (CIS): voluntary.** The record says "Responding to this survey is voluntary." The CIS is given to a sub-sample of LFS respondents. It also uses tax data from the Canada Revenue Agency.

- **Sample size:** The monthly LFS sample is about 65,000 households. That yields labour market information for about 100,000 individuals. Statistics Canada says the size can change to meet data quality, information or budget needs.
- **Reference week:** It is usually the week containing the 15th day of the month. That is the middle of the month, not a fixed week number. Collection takes place in the ten days right after the reference week.

**Where the income figures come from**

- Income and income-source amounts come from administrative tax data, not from respondents' answers. The Canada Revenue Agency's personal income data are linked to the survey records.
- Since reference year 2021, the source is the Administrative Personal Income Masterfile (APIM). It draws on T1 tax returns and the associated tax slips. Earlier years used T1 returns only.
- Survey interviews supply the other content: labour activity, housing costs, disability, food security and similar topics. Interviews are by person, by phone or by self-completed electronic questionnaire.
- Geography and many household characteristics come from the Labour Force Survey (LFS), because the CIS sample is a sub-sample of the LFS.
- From reference year 2022, "CIS-Plus" uses all LFS respondents. That more than doubles the sample for most published income and poverty tables.

**How sampling variance is estimated**

- Statistics Canada uses the bootstrap method. It produces a set of 1,000 bootstrap weights.
- A separate set of 1,000 bootstrap weights covers the disability and unmet health care needs content.
- Since CIS 2022, the CIS-Plus sample also has its own weight sets for the provinces.

**Housing start (Starts and Completions Survey, SCS):** CMHC counts a start when construction has reached the **beginning of construction of the building**. In practice, that is when the **concrete footing around the structure has been poured**, or an equivalent stage of construction. For a building with no concrete footing, it is the **equivalent stage of structural work**. Starts are counted by dwelling unit. Each unit in a multi-unit building is counted as a start once the building reaches this stage. The survey covers all dwelling types: single-detached, semi-detached, row, and apartment and other. For urban centres of 10,000 or more people, CMHC enumerates the starts directly. For smaller areas, it uses other methods.

**When:** CMHC runs the Rental Market Survey once a year, in the first two weeks of October. Results describe market conditions at that time, so a table labelled 2025 is the October 2025 survey. An April survey was also run in some years, but the last one was in 2015.

**What it covers:** the primary (purpose-built) rental market.
- It is a sample survey of urban areas with populations of 10,000 or more.
- It targets privately initiated structures with at least 3 rental units that have been on the market for at least 3 months.
- Apartment structures have 3 or more rental units, at least one of them not ground oriented.
- Row (townhouse) structures have 3 or more rental units, all ground oriented and side by side with common walls.
- Social and affordable housing is not in the survey frame.
- Owner-occupied units are not counted in a structure's rental unit count.

Other rentals fall under the separate Secondary Rental Market Survey. These include rented single-detached and semi-detached houses, duplexes, accessory apartments and rented condominiums. Since 2017 that survey has been limited to condominium apartments, collected in September in 17 CMAs.

**Where the income figures come from**
- Income and income-source data come mainly from administrative tax records from the Canada Revenue Agency, not from respondents' answers.
- Since reference year 2021, these come from the Administrative Personal Income Masterfile (APIM). It draws on T1 returns and the associated tax slips. Earlier years used T1 returns only.
- Survey interviews supply the other content: labour activity, disability, housing costs, food security and similar topics. Respondents answer by in-person interview, telephone, or an electronic questionnaire. Household and geographic characteristics come from the Labour Force Survey (LFS).
- The CIS is a sub-sample of LFS respondents. Since 2022, the "CIS-Plus" sample covers all LFS respondents and more than doubles the sample for income and poverty estimates.

**How sampling variance is estimated**
- Statistics Canada uses the bootstrap method, with 1,000 bootstrap weights.
- A separate set of 1,000 bootstrap weights covers the disability and unmet health care needs content. Since 2022, the CIS-Plus sample also has its own weight sets.

**Weighting, which the variance estimates build on**
- Weights start from the LFS sub-weights. They are inflated for non-response, then calibrated to population totals. Those totals are demographic counts by province and territory, age/gender and family size, plus some metropolitan areas. They also include APIM wage and salary distribution totals. Since 2022, social assistance recipient counts are included as well.

Source: Statistics Canada, Canadian Income Survey (IMDB survey record 5200), sections on data sources and estimation: https://www23.statcan.gc.ca/imdb/p2SV.pl?Function=getSurvey&SDDS=5200. The record's collection dates appear to refer to the 2025 reference year.

CMHC's Starts and Completions Survey (SCSS) defines a housing start as the **beginning of construction work on a building**. In practice, that means the **pouring of the concrete footing, or an equivalent stage, for the whole structure**. This is the definition as I remember it. I couldn't retrieve CMHC's wording through this server's tools, so please check it against the source below.

- **Unit of count:** each dwelling unit in the building is counted as a start. A building with several units adds all of them.
- **Equivalent stage:** if a building has no footing, such as a structure on a pad or raft, the start is when the equivalent base work begins. This covers the full-basement or foundation stage.
- **Scope:** the survey covers new construction of self-contained dwellings. Conversions and renovations of existing buildings are generally excluded.
- **Completion:** a dwelling is counted as complete when all construction work is finished, or at least 90% is done and the dwelling is ready to occupy.

**When:** CMHC runs the Rental Market Survey once a year, in the first two weeks of October. The results show market conditions at that time. An April survey was also run in some years, but the last one was in 2015.

**What it covers:** The survey covers the primary (purpose-built) rental market in urban areas with populations of 10,000 or more. It includes:
- **Apartment structures:** 3 or more rental units, at least one not ground-oriented.
- **Row (townhouse) structures:** 3 or more rental units, all ground-oriented, side by side with common walls.

The structures must be privately initiated and have been on the rental market for at least 3 months. Social and affordable housing is not in the survey frame.

Rented houses, condos, duplexes and accessory apartments fall under CMHC's separate Secondary Rental Market Survey, not this one.

**Reliability code D** means **Poor (use with caution)**. For averages and totals such as average rent, it applies when the coefficient of variation (CV) is over 7.5% and up to 10%. For vacancy and availability rates, CMHC also uses the sampling fraction and the size of the universe. The other codes are A (Excellent), B (Very good) and C (Good). An estimate is shown as `**` (suppressed) when it is too unreliable to publish. For averages, that means a CV over 10%.

**Release threshold:** CMHC releases an estimate only if it rests on **4 or more responding entities**. This is a confidentiality rule. Unit counts are always released, because they are counts and not estimates.

CMHC runs the Rental Market Survey (RMS) once a year, in the first two weeks of October. The results reflect market conditions at that time, so a table labelled 2025 is the October 2025 survey. CMHC also ran an April survey in some years, but the last one was in 2015.

**Structures covered:** the survey covers the primary, or purpose-built, rental market. - **Apartments:** 3 or more rental units, at least one of which is not ground-oriented.
- **Row (townhouse) structures:** 3 or more rental units, all ground-oriented and side by side with common walls.

- Social and affordable housing is outside the survey frame.
